Chapter 7: Navigating Relationships After Covert Abuse.
As your healing journey moves forward, you might notice your focus shifting—maybe from just surviving, to actually thinking about what it means to build or rebuild healthy relationships. If you’ve been through covert narcissistic abuse, you probably know all too well the scars it leaves behind. There’s the struggle to trust, the fear of letting your guard down, and that constant watchfulness for any hint of manipulation.
So, how do you step into new—or even old—relationships with both caution and courage? Let’s talk about that.
First, it really helps to be able to spot the difference between healthy and unhealthy relationship dynamics. This means tuning in to your own feelings, noticing those gut reactions, and being willing to see red flags for what they are. But it also means giving yourself the freedom to let real trust and connection grow, little by little.
Here are a few gentle guidelines that might make this process feel more manageable:
Pacing vulnerability—try sharing personal things gradually. Pay attention to how the other person responds when you set boundaries or share your needs. Are they respectful? Or do they push back?
Checking for reciprocity—healthy relationships are built on mutual respect, empathy, and effort from both sides. If you find yourself always giving or accommodating, it’s worth pausing to reflect on that balance.
Listening to your intuition—when something feels off, don’t ignore it. Honor that feeling and give yourself time to think things through before moving forward.
Practicing assertive communication—let people know what you need and where your limits are. And then see if those boundaries are actually respected.
Now, here’s something to pay attention to. Sometimes, old patterns from the past can sneak in without you even realizing it. If you’ve survived covert abuse, you might find yourself drawn to the same kinds of dynamics you’re trying to leave behind, just because they feel familiar. Bringing some gentle awareness to these patterns—maybe with the help of a therapist or a support group—can make it easier to break the cycle and make healthier choices.
Rebuilding trust, both in yourself and in others, isn’t something that happens overnight. It often starts in smaller, low-pressure relationships—like with acquaintances or coworkers—before moving into deeper connections. Every positive experience helps. Over time, you start to believe again that safe, supportive relationships really are possible.
If you think about it, this stage is a lot like learning to swim after almost drowning. At first, the water feels scary and dangerous. But with patience, and maybe a little support, your confidence grows. And before long, you find yourself enjoying the water again—the simple joy of human connection returning, one small step at a time.
